The light paper is the background: the main subject is drawn directly on it, large and central, its surroundings sketched in around it and fading into the paper, leaving open margins; insets are small ruled boxes on the same paper, each a clearly different moment or detail. Flat even diagram lighting, a quiet nostalgic warmth. People are ordinary Lithuanians of 1981, anonymous types with correct natural proportions, each person a different individual: fair skin, ash-blond to light-brown hair, grey or blue-grey eyes, broad-cheeked oval faces, straight noses, calm closed mouths, austere and plainly handsome. Men side-parted or cropped, some moustached, working men in flat caps; women blond or light-brown-haired, the younger ones lean, with hair mostly straight, now and then faintly waved or neatly styled; older women in the usual range of everyday styles, plain, pinned back or set, occasionally curled, or under a cotton headscarf; clothes plain and loosely cut, in brown, olive, dusty blue, grey and dull red, chosen for the setting and occasion. Heads turn at varied natural angles: in a group most look at their task or at each other and one or two face the viewer, eyes just past the viewer's shoulder; of two main figures only one faces the viewer; a lone figure stands near-frontal, face turned only a little. Subject: a passenger airplane. Main picture: an orange single-engine high-wing monoplane with wide aerofoil-shaped struts bracing the wing to the fuselage, a ring-cowled radial engine, a two-bladed propeller and fixed undercarriage with two spoked wheels, standing on a grass airfield before a wooden hangar; two men in leather flying jackets and soft flying helmets beside it, one checking the engine; the aircraft is the subject. Insets: the same plane in level flight over grey sea; the cockpit windows from outside; a passenger airliner of 1981 on an apron with a small tricolour on its tail. Keep the subject large and dominant in the foreground, floating cleanly on the cream paper on a simple background. This card quietly evokes a real Lithuanian precedent: an orange single-engine high-wing monoplane with wide aerofoil-shaped wing struts, a ring-cowled radial engine and two spoked wheels. It is carried by features alone - the shape and materials of the building, the cut and colour of period dress, the livery, struts and engine of an aircraft, the kit of a team - and never by lettering, a name, a plaque or a badge. The precedent sits inside the album's 1981 world and is drawn in the same flat matte ink as everything around it; it supports the card's word and does not replace it. The man checking the engine is drawn in the likeness of Steponas Darius as he looked in 1933: a man of 37 with a broad, square face, a strong jaw and a straight nose, light eyes under level brows, clean-shaven, in a leather flying jacket with a soft flying helmet pushed back. Carry the likeness in the face, hair, build and bearing, printed flat in the album style at the same scale as the other figures - a recognisable person drawn by the same anonymous hand, not a portrait. No name, caption, plaque or lettering identifies the person anywhere in the picture. The second man, beside the wing strut is drawn in the likeness of Stasys Girėnas as he looked in 1933: a man of 39 with a narrower, longer oval face, a long straight nose and a small firm mouth, clean-shaven, in the same leather flying kit. Carry the likeness in the face, hair, build and bearing, printed flat in the album style at the same scale as the other figures - a recognisable person drawn by the same anonymous hand, not a portrait. No name, caption, plaque or lettering identifies the person anywhere in the picture. The main picture alone makes this card's word obvious at a glance: the subject is the largest and most central element, shown in its most recognisable form and in the action that defines it, and the insets only add supporting detail. Any people who appear are ordinary Lithuanian civilians in plain everyday clothes of 1981, dressed for the setting and the weather: shirts, cardigans, simple dresses and headscarves indoors and on the street; coats, caps and hats outdoors in cold weather. Every person in a group is a different individual, with a distinct face, age, build, hair and clothing colour. Of two main figures, one faces the viewer with eyes resting just past the viewer's shoulder and the other looks at the task, at the first figure, or into the scene. Only include people the subject or scene actually calls for; do not add an extra standing figure that is not needed. Include small supporting insets exactly as listed after 'Insets:' in the staging above, each a different detail, angle or example; none repeats the main picture. All insets are drawn in the same thin ruled frame on the same paper, each showing a clearly different moment, object or angle from the others and from the main picture. Every inset must serve the meaning of THIS card: at best it should make the main subject easier to recognise; at the least it must stay attractive and on-theme. An inset must NEVER depict something that could be mistaken for a different, neighbouring subject, and must never compete with or pull attention away from what the card is teaching. Do NOT include internal anatomical cutaways or cross-sections of bodies — no organs, no digestive tracts, no bone interiors, no skin-layer diagrams, no udder or muscle interiors. Use external close-up details instead. (A simple sliced view of a fruit or plain object is fine.) Every object, tool and fixture is complete, attached and in working order: hanging things hang from a proper rack or hook, doorways and corridors stay clear and passable, furniture rests on the floor against a wall, tools are held in a usable grip, machines and vehicles are whole and correctly scaled to the people, and a resting animal is visibly alive and at ease, eyes closed and body relaxed. Wherever the card shows the same scene more than once - in two or more panels, in a strip, or in an inset that repeats the main scene - every repetition is the same place seen from a consistent viewpoint: the same people in the same clothes and the same relative positions (left stays left, nobody steps in front of or behind another, nobody enters or leaves), the same walls, doors, windows, furniture, counters, signs and street fixtures in the same places, and every object held by the same person unless the staging says it is handed over, and then both hands are on it. Only the moment changes: gesture, expression, the step of the action. An inset that shows a different place, object or close-up detail is not a repetition and is free. Every surface is dead-matte, as absorbent offset paper prints it: skin, hair, fabric, leather, metal, glass, water and polished wood carry flat ink tone and one soft shadow tone only. Any arrow or callout, drawn in solid black ink, points only at the subject the card teaches or at the direction of its motion. Render NO text, NO lettering, NO numbers, NO words, NO labels and NO captions anywhere in the image — no leader-line labels, no writing in any panel, on any flag, sign, or object, and none in the header or footer bands. Any area that would normally hold text must be left completely blank. This applies with full force inside speech bubbles and thought balloons: a bubble may contain a drawn picture or symbol, but never a written word, letter, or punctuation mark in any language. Frame the card with a plain solid deep, dark brick-red horizontal band across the very top and another across the very bottom, plus a thin band of the same dark red around the whole card. These bands are blank design elements and must contain no text whatsoever. Keep ALL illustration content — every figure, object, and inset panel — fully inside the inner frame; nothing may overlap, touch, or extend across the red header or footer bands. If any national emblem is shown at all, use ONLY a small Lithuanian tricolor flag (a horizontal yellow band on top, green in the middle, red on the bottom), placed small and only where it fits naturally. Do NOT include coats of arms, the Vytis knight, the Columns of Gediminas, or any other heraldic emblem or badge. Do not put a flag on every card — many cards need no emblem at all. Render any human hands with clean, natural anatomy and exactly five fingers, and render animal paws, hooves and feet cleanly and correctly — no extra or malformed fingers or toes. Finish: dead-matte offset print on light aged cream paper with a faint yellow cast, brush-ink outlines, soft shading, correct proportions, flat tone on skin, hair, cloth and metal. One or two faces toward the viewer, eyes just past the shoulder; of two main figures only one. Every inset a clearly different moment, all in the same ruled frame. Diagram arrows and callouts in solid black ink.
